The Prophet Muhammad

The Story of Islam

The Prophet Muhammad

The Meccan Years

In everyday English — the life that changed Mecca

Stories by Eku

How to Read · · BEFORE WE BEGIN

Read it out loud. This story was made to be told. Read slowly, as if you were sitting among family at home — with the lanes of Mecca, the caravan bells, and the silence of the mountains in the background.

The yellow boxes are the characters speaking in their own words. Change your voice a little when you read them — Khadija's gentle voice, Abu Talib's deep voice, young Ali's clear voice.

At the end of every part, the green box — Pause and think. Stop there. Ask questions. Let the listener speak. In this story, those questions matter as much as the story.

There are two kinds of things in this book — the Quran's verses and the evidence of history, such as the Hadith books and the ruins of old cities; and the stories of tradition, told in the books of the Seerah for centuries. Where a story comes from tradition, the book says so plainly — 'the tradition tells us'. Where something rests on evidence, the book names it.

There is no picture of the Prophet Muhammad in this book — not as a man, not as a child, not as an infant, not in shadow, not from behind. That is a mark of respect for Islamic tradition, and a rule of this whole series. Even in the chapter about the Cave of Hira, there is only the cave, the mountain, the light, and the sky.

This book's main story comes from the Quran, Ibn Ishaq's Seerah, the Hadith books, al-Tabari's History, and modern scholars. The full list of sources is at the end of the book.

Who's Who · · WHO'S WHO

Muhammad — of the Banu Hashim clan, of the Quraysh tribe. The hero of this book — but there is no picture of him anywhere in it.

Amina — daughter of Banu Zuhra, Muhammad's mother.

Halima — the wet-nurse of the Banu Sa'd tribe, who raised the young Muhammad in the desert — as the tradition tells it.

Abd al-Muttalib — chief of the Quraysh, Muhammad's grandfather.

Abu Talib — son of Abd al-Muttalib, Muhammad's uncle and protector; Ali's father.

Khadija — Mecca's most successful woman merchant, Muhammad's wife and his first companion.

Ali — son of Abu Talib, raised from childhood in Muhammad's house; among the first believers.

Abu Bakr — Muhammad's closest friend, an honest merchant, among the first believers.

Bilal — a slave from Abyssinia, freed by Abu Bakr — as the tradition tells it; among the first believers.

Zayd ibn Haritha — raised in Muhammad's house, freed by him and made his son — as the tradition tells it.

Waraqa ibn Nawfal — Khadija's cousin, a scholar of the old scriptures, counted among the hanifs.

The chiefs of the Quraysh — Abu Jahl, Abu Lahab, Utba ibn Rabi'a and Umayya ibn Khalaf — who became the fiercest opponents of the new message.

Mus'ab ibn Umayr — the first teacher sent to Yathrib, who taught people the Quran there.

1 · The Orphan Childhood — Amina, Halima and Abu Talib · · THE ORPHAN CHILDHOOD

The child born in Mecca in the Year of the Elephant — Muhammad — was born an orphan. The tradition tells us that his father Abdullah had already died before he was born — he fell ill at Yathrib on his way back from a trading journey and died there. His mother Amina was left alone, and his grandfather Abd al-Muttalib took the child to himself.

The tradition tells us that the child was sent to the desert to be nursed — to Halima, a wet-nurse of the Banu Sa'd tribe. The people of Mecca sent their children to the desert — so the child would grow up in clean air, speak pure Arabic, and grow strong. Halima took the child to her village, and he stayed there for some years. The tradition says blessing came to Halima's house — her goats gave more milk, her camels grew strong.

When the child was about five or six, he came back to Mecca. And then another sorrow came — the tradition tells us that his mother Amina took him to Yathrib to visit her family; on the way back, at a place called Abwa, she fell ill and died. The child was six years old — an orphan now of both mother and father. Umm Ayman, whom people also called Baraka — the old servant of the house — brought him back to Mecca, and became like a second mother to him.

His grandfather Abd al-Muttalib held the child close. The tradition tells us that the old chief would seat the boy on his own mat beside the Kaaba, and when someone said the child should move, the grandfather would say — let him be, this son of mine has a great destiny. But the grandfather did not live much longer either — about two years later, when the boy was eight, he too died.

Now the boy was taken in by his uncle Abu Talib. Abu Talib was not rich — he had many children, and the house was short of money. But he treated his nephew no less than his own children. The tradition tells us that when food was short, Abu Talib would feed his nephew first. The boy grew up in his uncle's house — herding goats, doing the work of the house, and growing up in the lanes of Mecca.

When the boy was nine or ten, his uncle took him on a caravan to Syria. It was his first great journey — from Mecca to the north, across the desert to the markets of Bosra. The tradition tells us that on the way, a Christian monk named Bahira saw the boy and told his uncle to guard him well, for his destiny was great.

The boy grew up — and the people of Mecca came to know him by one name — al-Amin, the Trustworthy. People left their valuables with him, and asked him to settle their disputes. The tradition tells us that when the Kaaba was repaired and there was a quarrel over who would set the Black Stone in place, it was he who found the answer — the stone was placed on a cloth, and the chief of every clan lifted one corner of it.

The dates of childhood — the tradition's dates

The year of Muhammad's birth, 570 CE (the Year of the Elephant), is the tradition's date — it is the year found in Ibn Ishaq's Seerah and al-Tabari's History. Modern scholars debate this date — some say the birth may have been a few years later, around 570. Abdullah dying before the birth, the nursing with Halima, Amina dying at Abwa, and the grandfather dying two years later — these are all stories from the Seerah; none of them has a document of its own from that time.

The story of Bahira the monk

Bahira the monk seeing the boy and speaking of his great destiny is a story from Ibn Ishaq's Seerah — a story of tradition. Modern scholars (such as W. Montgomery Watt) think it may be a story added later, told to show the boy's special nature from the start. In this book it is told with 'the tradition tells us'.

The quarrel over the Black Stone

The repair of the Kaaba and the settling of the quarrel over the Black Stone — the stone on a cloth, every chief lifting a corner — is a story from Ibn Ishaq's Seerah. It is told to show Muhammad's wisdom and the trust people placed in him.

Pause and think — A child — no father, no mother, no grandfather. And yet the people of Mecca called him al-Amin. Trust is not built on wealth — so what is it built on?

2 · Khadija — The Merchant, the Wife, the Companion · · KHADIJA — THE MERCHANT, THE WIFE, THE COMPANION

There was a woman in Mecca — Khadija bint Khuwaylid. She was Mecca's most successful merchant. Her caravans went to Syria and Yemen, and the great merchants of Mecca worked for her. She was a widow — twice married, both husbands dead — and now she ran her business herself.

Khadija needed a trustworthy man for her caravan. People told her the name of Muhammad — al-Amin, the Trustworthy. Khadija sent him with her caravan to Syria, and sent her servant Maysara with him — to see what kind of man he was.

The tradition tells us that Maysara came back and told Khadija — this man is not like the others. The caravan prospered, the trading went well, and on the road he saw strange things — as if the clouds walked along with him. Khadija listened, and she told her heart to her friend Nafisa. Nafisa went to Muhammad — and carried the proposal of marriage.

The tradition tells us that the marriage took place — Muhammad was twenty-five, and Khadija was older than him. After the marriage, Muhammad came to live in Khadija's house, and began to help her in her business. Their house became one of the most respected houses in Mecca — not only for its wealth, but for the trust people placed in it.

Many people grew up in their house — Zayd ibn Haritha, whom Muhammad had freed and made his son; Ali, the young son of Abu Talib, whom Muhammad took into his house because Abu Talib's house was short of money; and Umm Ayman, who still looked after the house.

The tradition tells us that they had several children — the sons Qasim and Abdullah, who died young; and the daughters Zaynab, Ruqayya, Umm Kulthum and Fatima. People sometimes called Muhammad Abu al-Qasim — father of Qasim.

That house ran for twenty-five years — and in those twenty-five years Khadija became Muhammad's greatest strength. When the first revelation came to him and he was afraid, it was to Khadija that he went first. But that is the story of the next part.

Khadija's age — two different tellings

How old Khadija was at the time of the marriage — on this the tradition gives two different tellings. The famous telling is that she was forty and Muhammad twenty-five — this is in Ibn Ishaq's Seerah. But some other traditions say she was twenty-eight — this is found in Ibn Sa'd and some other books. Modern scholars (such as Karen Armstrong) think the forty-year telling became more famous later, and the twenty-eight-year telling is just as old. In this book the main story gives no age — only that Khadija was older than him.

The number of children — a matter of tradition

The children's names — Qasim, Abdullah, Zaynab, Ruqayya, Umm Kulthum, Fatima — come from Ibn Ishaq's Seerah and the Hadith books. Some traditions also name another son, Tahir, and some take Abdullah and Tahir to be the same person. That is why the number of children differs a little between traditions — this book gives the most widely accepted list.

Pause and think — Khadija was Mecca's most successful merchant — and she married by her own wealth and her own choice. In the world of that time, how great a thing was that? And today?

3 · Cave Hira and the First Revelation — 610 · · CAVE HIRA AND THE FIRST REVELATION — 610

Muhammad was now close to forty. The tradition tells us that he had come to love being alone — he would leave Mecca and go into the mountains, and sit in a cave on Mount Hira and think. The cave was small — just enough for one man to sit. Below it lay the valley of Mecca; above it, the open sky.

The tradition tells us that in the month of Ramadan, one night, something happened in the cave. An angel came — Jibril. He said — 'Iqra!' — Read! Muhammad said — I do not know how to read. The angel seized him, pressed him hard, and said again — 'Iqra!'

And then came the words that are held to be the first words of the Quran — Surah al-Alaq (96:1-5):

Read, in the name of your Lord who created —

who created man from a clinging clot.

Read, and your Lord is most Generous —

who taught by the pen, taught man what he did not know.

The tradition tells us that Muhammad came out of the cave trembling with fear and ran home. He went to Khadija and said — cover me, cover me. Khadija covered him with a blanket, comforted him, and said —

Khadija: By God, God will never disgrace you. You look after your family, you speak the truth, you honour your guests, and you help people in trouble.

Khadija took him to her cousin Waraqa ibn Nawfal. Waraqa was a scholar of the old scriptures — he read the Torah and the Gospel. The tradition tells us that Waraqa listened to Muhammad and said — this is the same angel who came to Moses. I wish I could be alive on the day your people drive you out.

And then, for a time, the revelation stopped — the tradition calls this fatrat al-wahy, the pause in revelation. Muhammad was restless — and then the revelation came again, and never stopped again.

The first revelation — the Quran's own words and the Seerah's story

The words of the first revelation — Surah al-Alaq (96:1-5) — are the Quran's own words; Muslims hold them to be the first verses of the Quran to be revealed. Jibril coming in the cave, the command 'Iqra', and Muhammad running home in fear — all of this is the story of Ibn Ishaq's Seerah and Sahih al-Bukhari — a story of tradition, told by Muslims for centuries. Khadija's words and Waraqa's words are also in Sahih al-Bukhari. In this book the verses of the Quran are given as the Quran's own words, and the rest of the story as tradition.

The date 610

The year of the first revelation, 610 CE, is the tradition's date — it is the year found in the books of the Seerah, in the month of Ramadan. This date too comes from tradition; no document of that time survives.

Pause and think — The first word was — 'Read'. It was spoken to a man who did not know how to read. Why? Is reading only about reading a book — or is it something more?

4 · The First Believers — Khadija, Ali, Abu Bakr, Zayd, Bilal · · THE FIRST BELIEVERS

After the first revelation, Muhammad spoke first in his own house. And the first to believe what he said was — Khadija. The tradition tells us that Khadija became the first Muslim — she said without hesitation that what he had seen was true.

The second was — Ali. Ali was then about ten years old, and was growing up in Muhammad's house. The tradition tells us that Ali saw Muhammad and Khadija praying and asked — what is this? Muhammad told him — this is the worship of God. Ali said — I will ask my father and tell you. Then he thought all night, and in the morning he said — I do not need to ask my father, I believe.

The third was — Zayd ibn Haritha, who belonged to the house, and whom Muhammad had freed and made his son.

And then came — Abu Bakr. Abu Bakr was Muhammad's closest friend, an honest merchant of Mecca, whose word everyone trusted. The tradition tells us that when Muhammad told him his message, Abu Bakr did not think for a moment — he believed at once. And then Abu Bakr went to his friends — Uthman, Zubayr, Abd al-Rahman ibn Awf, Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas and Talha — and they too believed.

And there was one more — Bilal. Bilal was from Abyssinia, and a slave in Mecca. The tradition tells us that Bilal too heard the message and believed — and later Abu Bakr set him free.

At first all of this happened quietly — inside houses, in the dark of night, in small gatherings. The tradition tells us that for the first three years the message reached only close people. Then the day came when the command came — now say it before everyone. That is the story of the next part.

The first believers — the tradition's list

Khadija, Ali, Zayd and Abu Bakr being the first to believe is told in Ibn Ishaq's Seerah and the Hadith books. Ali's age at that time is given as about ten — this too is a matter of tradition. Bilal being freed by Abu Bakr is also a story from the Seerah. Uthman, Zubayr, Abd al-Rahman, Sa'd and Talha believing through Abu Bakr also comes from tradition. None of these has a document of its own from that time.

Pause and think — The first believers were no kings, no chiefs — a wife, a child, a friend, a slave. Do great changes always begin with great people — or sometimes with small ones too?

5 · The Public Call — Mount Safa, the Message and the Opposition · · THE PUBLIC CALL — SAFA

◆ This part is not for younger listeners

The tradition tells us that after three years of quiet teaching, the command came — now say it before everyone. Muhammad climbed Mount Safa and called out to the people of Mecca — O Quraysh, O Banu Hashim, O Banu Abd Manaf! The people gathered — what is it, what do you have to say?

The tradition tells us that Muhammad said — if I told you that behind this hill there is an army about to attack you, would you believe me? The people said — yes, you are al-Amin, you have never lied. Then Muhammad said — then listen, I warn you of a great punishment — God is One, and I am His Messenger.

The tradition tells us that among the first to speak was — Abu Lahab, Muhammad's own uncle. He said — may you perish, is this why you called us? And he got up and left.

After that day Mecca changed. The day before, people had called Muhammad al-Amin — now the chiefs of the Quraysh began to call him an enemy. Abu Jahl, Abu Lahab, Utba ibn Rabi'a and Umayya ibn Khalaf — these were the chiefs, and they said that this new message would destroy Mecca's old ways, the worship of the Kaaba, and the honour of the tribes — all of it.

First they mocked him, then they threatened him, then they began to persecute. Those who were poor, who were slaves, who had no tribe — they suffered the most. The tradition tells us that Bilal was laid by his master Umayya on the burning sand of the desert, a heavy stone placed on his chest, and told — believe in Lat and Uzza. Bilal said one word — Ahad, Ahad — One, One. This is said here in a single line, without a picture, because it is not for younger listeners.

The tradition tells us that Sumayya and Yasir — an old mother and father — were also killed in this persecution. They are counted as the first martyrs of Islam. This too is said here in a single line.

And those who could not stay in Mecca left — the tradition tells us that in 615 CE a small group of Muslims crossed the sea to Abyssinia, where the Christian king the Negus ruled. The Negus gave them shelter. This was the first hijra of Islam — but the story of Mecca was not yet over.

Those who stayed in Mecca met in secret — in Dar al-Arqam, the house of Arqam, near Mount Safa. There they prayed, listened to the Quran, and gave each other courage.

The call on Safa — a story from the Hadith

The story of the call on Mount Safa — 'if I told you there is an army behind this hill' — is in Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim. Abu Lahab's answer is also in the Hadith books. Surah al-Masad (111) of the Quran mentions Abu Lahab.

Bilal, Sumayya and Yasir — the tradition's story

The story of the persecution of Bilal — laid on the sand, the stone on his chest, and 'Ahad, Ahad' — is from Ibn Ishaq's Seerah. The killing of Sumayya and Yasir is also from the Seerah — they are counted as the first martyrs of Islam. These stories have no document of their own from that time; they are matters of tradition, and in this book they are told in a line or two, without a picture.

The migration to Abyssinia — 615

The year of the first migration to Abyssinia, 615 CE, is the tradition's date — it is the year found in the books of the Seerah. The Negus giving shelter to the Muslims is also a story from Ibn Ishaq's Seerah.

Pause and think — The man who was al-Amin yesterday — how did he become an enemy today? Did people change him — or did their own fear?

6 · The Boycott — Three Hard Years in the Valley of Abu Talib · · THE BOYCOTT — THREE HARD YEARS IN THE VALLEY

◆ This part is not for younger listeners

The tradition tells us that when mockery and persecution did not work, the chiefs of the Quraysh tried another way — the boycott. They wrote a document — no one would marry into Banu Hashim and Banu al-Muttalib, no one would trade with them, no one would sell them food, no one would speak to them. Until they handed Muhammad over to us.

The tradition tells us that this document was hung inside the Kaaba — so that all could see it, and all would obey it. And the people of Banu Hashim — Muslims or not — all had to leave Mecca and go to the valley of Abu Talib (Shi'b Abi Talib). That valley was a narrow place outside Mecca, between the mountains.

Three years — the tradition tells us that those three years were very hard. Food was short, water was short, and no trade came from outside. Children cried with hunger — this is said here in a single line. Sometimes a kind merchant would quietly bring food in the dark of night — the tradition tells us that Hisham ibn Amr was one such man, who carried food to the valley on his camel.

But the people of the valley did not give in. Abu Talib guarded his nephew — the tradition tells us that at night he would change his nephew's sleeping place, so that no one could kill him. And Muhammad gave his people courage — he said this time too would pass.

The tradition tells us that after three years, the boycott broke. The document hung in the Kaaba had been eaten by termites — only the name of Allah was left. And some people in Mecca itself — Hisham ibn Amr and his companions — had come to feel that this boycott was wrong. They told the Quraysh — this document is gone, and this boycott should end too. And the boycott broke. The people came back from the valley to Mecca.

The details of the boycott — the Seerah's story

The whole story of the boycott — the document, its hanging in the Kaaba, the three years in the valley, the termites eating the document, and Hisham ibn Amr bringing food — comes from Ibn Ishaq's Seerah. This story has no document of its own from that time; its details are matters of tradition, and in this book they are told as tradition. Modern scholars (such as W. Montgomery Watt) think the boycott truly happened, but its details may carry the colour of later stories.

The date of the three years

The years of the boycott are given in tradition as about 616 to 619 CE. This date too is a matter of tradition — from the books of the Seerah.

Pause and think — A whole people cut off food and water from one clan — so that they would hand over one of their own. And the clan did not break. What was it that held them together — blood, or something more?

7 · The Year of Sorrow — Khadija and Abu Talib Die · · THE YEAR OF SORROW

Not long after the return from the valley, two great sorrows came, one after the other. The tradition tells us that first Abu Talib died — the uncle who had raised the child, who had guarded him in the valley, who had stood before the Quraysh and said that no one would touch his nephew.

And not long after him died — Khadija. The wife who had covered Muhammad with a blanket on the night of the first revelation, who had shared her wealth and her life with him, who had been his greatest strength for twenty-five years.

The tradition calls this year — Aam al-Huzn, the Year of Sorrow. In a single year Muhammad lost his two greatest supports — one had guarded him from outside, the other had held him from within.

After Abu Talib died, Muhammad's protection in Mecca grew weak. The tradition tells us that the chiefs of the Quraysh grew bolder — there was no one left to hold them back. One day someone threw dust on Muhammad's head in a lane of Mecca — and when he came home, one of his daughters wiped the dust from his head, weeping.

The tradition tells us that Abu Lahab guarded Muhammad for a time — as an uncle should — but when he learned that Muhammad spoke against his gods, he too took his protection back.

In the Year of Sorrow Muhammad was left alone — but he did not give up his message. He went outside Mecca too — in the days of the pilgrimage, meeting the tribes that came, asking them whether there was anyone who would listen to his message. But that is the story of the coming parts.

The Year of Sorrow — a name from later tradition

The name 'Aam al-Huzn' (the Year of Sorrow) comes from later tradition — it is found in the books of the Seerah, but in no document of that time. Abu Talib and Khadija dying in the same year is also from Ibn Ishaq's Seerah. The year of their deaths is given in tradition as 619 CE — this date too is a matter of tradition.

Pause and think — In one year both supports were gone — one from outside, one from within. When everything is taken away, what does a person stand on?

8 · Taif — The Journey, the Rejection, the Garden · · TAIF — THE JOURNEY, THE REJECTION, THE GARDEN

◆ This part is not for younger listeners

After the Year of Sorrow, Muhammad looked outside Mecca — towards Taif. Taif was about sixty miles from Mecca, a green town in the mountains — full of gardens of grapes and fruit. The Thaqif tribe lived there. Muhammad thought — perhaps the people there would listen to my message.

The tradition tells us that Muhammad walked to Taif — with him was Zayd ibn Haritha. He spoke to the chiefs of Thaqif — told them his message, and asked them for help. But the chiefs refused — and not only refused.

The tradition tells us that they stirred up the people of the town, and Muhammad was driven out of the city — stones were thrown at him. This is said here in a single line, without a picture, because it is not for younger listeners. Zayd tried to shield him with his own body.

The tradition tells us that Muhammad sat down in a garden — the garden of Utba and Shayba, two chiefs of Mecca. There he made a prayer that is famous in the books of the Seerah — O God, to You I complain of my weakness, and of how helpless I look before people. You are the Lord of the weak, You are my Lord.

The tradition tells us that there was a slave in the garden — Addas, who had come from Nineveh (in today's Iraq) and was a Christian. Utba and Shayba sent him with a branch of grapes to Muhammad. Addas spoke with Muhammad, and the tradition tells us that he was so moved by his words that he kissed his hands.

Muhammad came back from Taif — empty-handed, but not defeated. The tradition tells us that on the way back he felt that his message would go beyond Mecca too — only the road had not yet shown itself.

The story of Taif — the tradition's telling

The journey to Taif, the chiefs of Thaqif refusing, the stones being thrown, the prayer in the garden, and the story of Addas — all of this is from Ibn Ishaq's Seerah. The prayer in the garden is also in the books of the Seerah — its words come from tradition. The year of the journey to Taif is given in tradition as 619 or 620 CE — this date too is a matter of tradition. In this book the throwing of stones is told in a single line, without a picture.

Pause and think — In Taif everything went wrong — refusal, stones, disgrace. And yet Muhammad sat in the garden and prayed, he did not answer with anger. Prayer instead of anger — is that defeat, or strength?

9 · The Night Journey — Isra and Mi'raj · · THE NIGHT JOURNEY — ISRA AND MI'RAJ

The tradition tells us that after the return from Taif, one night something happened that is one of the most famous stories of Islam — Isra and Mi'raj, the Night Journey.

The Quran speaks of this night in a single verse — Surah al-Isra (17:1): 'Glory be to Him who took His servant by night from the Sacred Mosque to the Farthest Mosque.' That is all — the Quran says nothing more than this. Everything else is the story of tradition.

The tradition tells us that on that night a mount came — the Buraq — a mount that moved faster than lightning. On it Muhammad went from Mecca to Jerusalem (Bayt al-Maqdis), prayed there, and then rose up through the heavens — passing through heaven after heaven, where he met the prophets of old — Adam, Jesus, Moses, Abraham.

The tradition tells us that there, at the highest place, he was given the command of the five daily prayers. At first fifty prayers were spoken of — the tradition tells us that Moses advised him that his people could not pray so many, to go back and ask for fewer — and so five remained.

In the morning, when Muhammad told the people of Mecca about this, many mocked him — Jerusalem and the heavens in a single night? The tradition tells us that Abu Bakr said — if he said it, then he has spoken the truth. That is why Abu Bakr came to be called al-Siddiq, the Truthful.

The Night Journey — the tradition's story and the scholars' debate

The story of the Night Journey — the Buraq, Jerusalem, the journey through the heavens, the meeting with the prophets, and the five daily prayers — comes from the Hadith books (Sahih al-Bukhari, Sahih Muslim) and Ibn Ishaq's Seerah. In the Quran there is only the single verse of Surah al-Isra (17:1) — the journey to Jerusalem; the journey through the heavens is not told in the Quran in this way.

Was it a physical journey or a vision?

Muslim scholars have long debated this — was the Night Journey physical (it happened with the body) or spiritual (a dream or a journey of the soul)? Some scholars say it was a physical journey; some say it was a dream or a spiritual experience. Modern scholars (such as Karen Armstrong and Fred Donner) record this debate honestly — and this book records it too. This book does not decide which telling is right — the story is told as tradition tells it, and the debate is recorded in a separate note.

The date of the Night Journey

The year of the Night Journey is given differently in tradition — 620 or 621 CE, one or two years before the Hijra. This date too is a matter of tradition; no document of that time survives.

Pause and think — In the Quran there is only one verse — and in tradition a whole story. Can a whole story grow from one verse? And when people argue about something, what should we do — decide, or listen to both sides?

10 · The Pledges of Aqaba — Yathrib Opens Its Doors · · THE PLEDGES OF AQABA — YATHRIB OPENS ITS DOORS

In Mecca there was still no place — but outside Mecca, there was a city that was listening — Yathrib. Yathrib was about two hundred and fifty miles north of Mecca, an oasis of palm gardens. The tribes of Aws and Khazraj lived there, and for years there had been war between them.

The tradition tells us that in 620 CE, in the days of the pilgrimage, some people of Yathrib came to Mecca and met Muhammad — at a place called Aqaba, a valley outside Mecca. They were six men, of the Khazraj tribe. They heard Muhammad's message, believed, and said — we will go back to our city and tell the people.

The next year, in 621 CE, they met again at Aqaba — this time there were twelve people. They promised — we will believe in one God, we will not steal, we will not lie, we will not kill our children. This was called the First Pledge of Aqaba.

The tradition tells us that Muhammad sent Mus'ab ibn Umayr with them to Yathrib — to teach the Quran and explain it to people. Mus'ab went to Yathrib, went from house to house telling people, and slowly people began to believe — great chiefs like Sa'd ibn Mu'adh and Usayd ibn Hudayr too.

And then came the pilgrimage of 622 CE — and a third meeting at Aqaba. This time there were seventy-three men and two women. In the dark of night, quietly, they made the second promise — the Second Pledge of Aqaba. They said — we will protect you as we protect our own children. We call you to our city — come, Yathrib is your home.

The tradition tells us that Muhammad said — then come, but slowly, in small groups, so that the Quraysh do not know. And the Muslims began to leave Mecca quietly — one by one, in the dark of night, towards Yathrib. This was the Hijra — and its story is in the next book.

The numbers at Aqaba — a matter of tradition

The numbers of the three meetings at Aqaba — six people, then twelve, then seventy-three men and two women — come from Ibn Ishaq's Seerah. In some traditions the numbers differ a little — seventy-two or seventy-five people are also given for the second pledge. This book gives the most widely accepted numbers, and this note records that the numbers differ slightly.

The dates of the pledges of Aqaba

The years of the pledges of Aqaba — 620, 621 and 622 CE — are the tradition's dates, from the books of the Seerah. The year of the Hijra, 622 CE, is also the start of the Muslim calendar.

Pause and think — The people of Yathrib had not fought the people of Mecca — they fought each other. And yet they gave their city to a stranger. What was it that they saw in Muhammad — and the chiefs of Mecca did not see?

Closing Reflection · · CLOSING REFLECTION

In this book we have seen a life — from an orphan childhood to Khadija's house, from the night in the Cave of Hira to the pledges of Aqaba. Thirteen years — and in those thirteen years Mecca saw a man who was first al-Amin, then an enemy, then left alone, and yet did not stop.

In this book we have also seen the people who stood with him — Khadija, who covered him with a blanket on the first night; Abu Talib, who guarded him in the valley; Abu Bakr, who believed in a single moment; Ali, who showed courage as a child; Bilal, who said 'Ahad' even under the stone.

In the next book we will hear the story of the Hijra — the journey from Mecca to Medina, and the city that became the start of a new society. But before that, take one question with you —

When everything is taken away — home, city, supports — what remains is the real wealth. What is your real wealth?

Pause and think — What touched you most in this book — the orphan childhood, Khadija's companionship, the night in the Cave of Hira, the three years in the valley, or the pledges of Aqaba? And why?

Sources · · SOURCES

The Quran — Surah al-Alaq (96:1-5), Surah al-Isra (17:1), Surah al-Masad (111), Surah al-Fil (105), Surah Quraysh (106).

Ibn Ishaq's Seerah (in the recension of Ibn Hisham) — the oldest book of the Seerah; most of the tradition-stories in this book come from it — the childhood, Khadija, the first revelation, the boycott, Taif, Aqaba.

Sahih al-Bukhari — a book of Hadith; the story of the first revelation (Khadija's words, Waraqa's words) and the story of the call on Safa are taken from it.

Sahih Muslim — a book of Hadith; the stories of the call on Safa and the Night Journey are also taken from it.

Al-Tabari's History (Tarikh al-Rusul wa al-Muluk) — on the order of dates and events.

Ibn Sa'd, Kitab al-Tabaqat — the second telling of Khadija's age (twenty-eight years) comes from it.

Fred Donner, Muhammad and the Believers — a modern scholar; on early Islam and the society of Mecca.

Karen Armstrong, Muhammad: A Prophet for Our Time — a biography of Muhammad, keeping tradition and history apart; on the debate over the Night Journey.

Lesley Hazleton, The First Muslim — a biography of Muhammad, on Khadija and the first believers.

W. Montgomery Watt, Muhammad at Mecca — the most trusted modern history of the Meccan years; on the boycott and the story of Bahira.

Wherever this book says 'the tradition tells us', the matter comes from the books of the Seerah and Hadith — not from the evidence of history. Where a matter rests on evidence, its name is given in a separate note.
